speaker_role: independent counselor/founder of a scholarship coaching business
commercial_incentive: Yes - founder of 'The Scholarship System'/'debt-free degree lab', repeatedly promotes her free training, playlist, and paid coaching program
key_insights: FAFSA opens October 1st of senior year; speaker recommends submitting within a few weeks after that (by end of October) rather than exactly on day one to avoid site overload
Some individual schools set FAFSA deadlines much earlier than the traditional tax-deadline rule of thumb, as early as December of senior year
Some state and institutional aid is awarded first-come-first-served, so later filers can lose out on aid even if otherwise eligible
Filing early leaves time to correct errors (e.g. mistaken tax figures) before the school finalizes the aid package in spring
Families should file FAFSA even if they expect to be ineligible, because many schools require it on file before offering any institutional aid, including need-blind merit funds
Even high-income families sometimes qualify for federal loans through FAFSA, which typically carry better terms than private loans
Some schools offer 'gap scholarships' that cover the difference between the FAFSA-calculated affordability and the actual bill, which can't be accessed without filing
FAFSA must be refiled every year because required income/asset data changes annually, and because a family's relative aid eligibility shifts as the applicant pool's demographics change each year
specific_numbers_or_facts: Some institutions set FAFSA deadlines as early as December of senior year, per speaker
Speaker cites having seen students miss around $40,000/year in aid by missing a school-specific FAFSA deadline
notable_or_distinctive: Explains the less commonly discussed 'gap scholarship' concept and the year-to-year relative-poverty reshuffling effect (aid can change even if your own finances haven't, because the rest of the applicant pool changed).
reliability_notes: Heavily promotional (multiple plugs for the presenter's paid program and free lead-magnet training); the $40,000/year missed-aid figure is an anecdotal claim without a named source or year.
